title: Kant II: The Categorical Imperative
subtitle: A morality that holds for every rational being, whatever they happen to want
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why Kant thought the good will is the only thing good without qualification.
By the end you will be able to distinguish acting from duty from acting merely in accordance with duty.
By the end you will be able to contrast hypothetical and categorical imperatives.
By the end you will be able to apply the Formula of Universal Law and the Formula of Humanity to real cases.
By the end you will be able to assess the famous objection from the murderer at the door.
hook:
Imagine a shopkeeper who never cheats his customers. A child comes in alone to buy bread, and he could easily overcharge her; she would never know. He gives her the correct change. Is he a good man?

You probably want to ask a follow-up question: *why* did he give the correct change? If he was honest only because word gets around and cheating children is bad for business, then he did the right thing, but it is hard to feel moral admiration. He would have cheated if he were sure he could get away with it. This little example comes from Kant himself, and it opens the door to one of the most demanding and influential moral theories ever written. For Kant, the moral worth of an action lies not in its results, and not in the warm feelings behind it, but in the principle the agent acts on. And the supreme principle of morality, he argued, can be discovered by reason alone — a single command binding on every rational being in the universe.

sections.heading: From Starry Heavens to the Moral Law
sections.body:
Yesterday (Day 55) we saw Kant limit knowledge to the world of appearances, where everything is governed by causal law. That left an urgent question. If every event in nature is causally determined, including the movements of my body, how can I be free? And if I am not free, how can I be responsible?

Kant's answer was that freedom cannot be known, but it must be presupposed whenever we act. When you deliberate about whether to keep a promise, you cannot treat your decision as something you will merely observe happening. You must act “under the idea of freedom”. And that freedom shows itself most clearly in our awareness of moral obligation: when I realize that I *ought* to do something even against all my desires, I discover that I am not just a bundle of desires pushed around by nature.

Kant set out his ethics in three main works: the short *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785), the *Critique of Practical Reason* (1788), and the longer *Metaphysics of Morals* (1797). The *Groundwork* is the one everyone reads, and it is our main text today. The conclusion of the second *Critique* contains his most famous sentence, later carved on a memorial plaque in Königsberg: two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the more often and steadily we reflect on them — the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.

That pairing captures Kant's whole outlook. The heavens are the realm of natural law that Newton revealed. The moral law is the realm of freedom. Both are lawful, both are universal, and both inspire reverence.

sections.heading: The Good Will and the Motive of Duty
sections.body:
The *Groundwork* opens with a bold claim:

> It is impossible to think of anything at all in the world, or indeed even beyond it, that could be considered good without limitation except a good will.

Think of all the things we normally call good: intelligence, courage, wealth, health, even happiness. Kant points out that every one of them can be turned to evil. A courageous, clever villain is more dangerous than a cowardly, stupid one. Even happiness can make people arrogant. Only a **good will** — the settled commitment to do what is right because it is right — is good in every circumstance. And it is good in itself, not because of what it achieves. Kant says that even if a good will, through bad luck, achieved nothing at all, it would still shine like a jewel, as something that has its full worth in itself.

What makes a will good? Acting from **duty**. Here Kant draws a sharp and much-discussed distinction. The shopkeeper acts *in accordance with* duty: he does the right thing, but from self-interest. Kant also asks us to consider a naturally sympathetic person who loves to help others because it gives her pleasure. Her actions are kind and deserve praise and encouragement, Kant says, but they lack genuine *moral worth*, because she would act the same way whether or not it was right. Now imagine that grief has numbed her and she no longer feels any pleasure in helping, but she helps anyway, simply because she recognizes she ought to. *Now*, Kant says, her action has moral worth.

This is one of the most controversial passages in ethics. It seems to say that cold duty is better than warm love. The poet Friedrich Schiller mocked it in a satirical verse, in which a man worries that because he enjoys helping his friends, he is not virtuous, and is told that he must learn to despise them first and then do his duty with disgust. Many Kant scholars think this is a misreading. Kant does not say feelings are bad, or that we should try to get rid of them. His point is about which motive is doing the work: an action has moral worth when the recognition of duty would have been enough to produce it. The hard cases are just where that motive becomes visible.

sections.heading: Two Kinds of “Ought”: Hypothetical and Categorical
sections.body:
Kant calls a command of reason an **imperative**. There are two kinds.

A **hypothetical imperative** tells you what to do *if* you want something. “If you want to pass the exam, study.” “If you want to stay healthy, exercise.” These are perfectly rational commands, but they are conditional. If you do not care about the exam, the command has no grip on you. Most of the practical advice in life — engineering, medicine, business — consists of hypothetical imperatives.

A **categorical imperative** commands unconditionally, regardless of what you happen to want. “Do not lie.” It does not say “do not lie if you want to keep your reputation”. It binds you even if lying would get you everything you desire. Kant thought that morality must take this form. If moral rules were just hypothetical — be honest *if* you want people to trust you — then someone with different goals could escape them. But we do not think a murderer escapes the wrongness of murder just because he does not care about being good.

This contrast puts Kant in direct opposition to Hume (Day 50), who said that reason is the slave of the passions: reason can only tell us how to get what we already desire. Kant insists that pure practical reason can itself command. It also sets him against the utilitarians we will meet on Day 61, for whom the rightness of an act depends entirely on its consequences. For Kant, consequences belong to the world of luck. Morality lies in the principle you act on.

That principle Kant calls a **maxim**: the personal rule or policy behind an action, such as “when I need money, I will borrow it and promise to repay, even though I know I can't”. The categorical imperative is a test for maxims.

sections.heading: The Formula of Universal Law
sections.body:
Kant states the categorical imperative in several ways, which he claimed were different expressions of one and the same law. The first and most famous is the **Formula of Universal Law**:

> Act only in accordance with that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law.

The test works like this. Take your maxim and imagine it as a law of nature that everyone follows. Then ask two questions. Can such a world even be coherently conceived? And if it can, could you consistently *will* to live in it?

Kant's most famous example is the lying promise. Suppose my maxim is to make false promises whenever I need money. Universalize it: everyone makes false promises whenever they need money. In such a world, promises would be worthless; nobody would believe them, and the practice of promising would collapse. But then my maxim defeats itself: I can only succeed in deceiving by a promise if most people keep their promises. My maxim requires a world in which others do not act as I do. That is a **contradiction in conception**, and it reveals a strict or “perfect” duty: never make false promises.

Other maxims can be universalized without contradiction, but cannot be consistently willed. Kant's example is a prosperous man who decides never to help anyone in need. A world where nobody helps anybody is conceivable. But no rational person could will it, because every one of us may one day need help, and in willing this world we would be willing to be abandoned. This is a **contradiction in the will**, and it reveals a looser or “imperfect” duty: help others sometimes, though you have some freedom in when and how.

The key insight here is about fairness. When we act wrongly, Kant suggests, we usually do not want our maxim to become universal. We want everyone else to follow the rule, while we make an exception for ourselves. The categorical imperative catches the free rider. This is close to, but not the same as, the Golden Rule (“do as you would be done by”), which Kant explicitly said was inadequate because it depends on what particular people happen to want.

sections.heading: The Formula of Humanity
sections.body:
Kant's second major formulation is, for many readers, the most inspiring sentence in modern ethics. It is called the **Formula of Humanity**:

> So act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.

To treat someone **merely as a means** is to use them as a tool for your purposes in a way they could not possibly share or agree to. The false promiser does this: he uses the lender's trust as a mere instrument, and the lender cannot consent to a plan whose whole success depends on his being deceived. Fraud, coercion, manipulation and slavery are the clearest cases.

Notice the word *merely*. Kant does not forbid using people as means at all; we do it constantly. When you buy coffee, you use the barista as a means to get coffee, and she uses you as a means to earn a living. That is fine, as long as you also respect her as an **end in herself**: a rational being who sets her own goals, who has agreed to the exchange, and whom you would not deceive or force.

Why do people deserve this respect? Because they are rational agents capable of setting ends and giving themselves the moral law. Kant calls this **autonomy**, literally “self-legislation”. Things in the market have a *price*: they can be exchanged for something of equal value. But a rational being has *dignity*, a worth beyond all price, which cannot be traded away. This idea is a direct ancestor of modern human rights. Kant's third formulation pictures morality as a **kingdom of ends**: an ideal community in which every member is both a lawmaker and subject to the laws, and everyone is respected as an end.

Note too that the Formula of Humanity includes “your own person”. Kant thought we have duties to ourselves — not to destroy ourselves, not to degrade ourselves, to develop our talents — because the humanity in us also deserves respect.

sections.heading: The Murderer at the Door, and Other Objections
sections.body:
Kant's theory faces a famous test case. Suppose your friend is hiding in your house, and a murderer knocks at the door and asks where he is. May you lie?

Almost everyone says yes. Kant, notoriously, said no. In a short essay of 1797, *On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy*, he replied to the French writer Benjamin Constant, who had used exactly this kind of case against strict truthfulness. Kant argued that truthfulness is an unconditional duty, and that if you lie, you make yourself responsible for whatever follows; if you tell the truth and something bad happens, it is the murderer's doing. He even imagined that your friend might have slipped out of the house, so that your lie sends the murderer straight to him.

Many readers find this a reductio, a sign that something is badly wrong with the theory. Kant's defenders offer several replies. Christine Korsgaard has argued that the Formula of Universal Law, properly applied, actually *permits* the lie: the maxim “lie to murderers who deceive you about their intentions” can be universalized without contradiction, because the murderer is himself exploiting your honesty. Others say Kant's essay is about lying in a legal and political context, not personal ethics. Still others accept that Kant himself was too rigid but that his framework can handle the case.

There are deeper objections too:

- **Empty formalism.** Hegel (Day 59) argued that the universal law test is purely formal and can be made to approve almost anything if you describe the maxim cleverly enough.
- **Conflicting duties.** What should you do when two strict duties clash, such as keeping a promise and saving a life? Kant gives little guidance.
- **Coldness.** Care ethicists (Day 85) and virtue ethicists object that an ethics centred on duty and rules misses the moral importance of love, relationships and character.
- **Who counts?** If dignity rests on rationality, what about infants, people with severe cognitive disabilities, or animals? Kant held that we have no direct duties to animals, only a duty not to become cruel. Many find this troubling.

Yet Kant's core ideas — that morality must be fair and universal, that people are not tools, that each person has a dignity that cannot be traded off — remain central to moral and political thought, from John Rawls (Day 82) to the language of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Tomorrow we see how Kant took these ideas into politics.

keyQuote.text: So act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.
keyQuote.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785), Section II

modernConnection.title: Informed Consent and Dark Patterns
modernConnection.body:
If you have ever signed a consent form before surgery or a medical study, you have met Kant's Formula of Humanity in institutional form. Modern research ethics grew out of horror at scientific abuses — the Nazi experiments judged at Nuremberg, and in the United States the Tuskegee study, in which Black men with syphilis were deliberately left untreated for decades. The 1979 Belmont Report, which shapes U.S. research rules, lists “respect for persons” as its first principle: people must be treated as autonomous agents and must be allowed to decide for themselves, with full information, whether to take part. That is almost exactly Kant's demand that we never use someone merely as a means. Deceiving a patient into a trial is a lying promise in a white coat.

The same principle gives a sharp tool for judging technology. Designers talk about **dark patterns**: interface tricks that steer users into choices they would not make if they understood them. Think of a subscription that takes one click to start and a maze of screens to cancel, pre-ticked boxes that share your data, or countdown timers that create fake urgency. A Kantian test is simple: could the user consent to this design if they saw exactly how it works? If the trick only succeeds because the user does not understand it, it treats them as a mere means. Universalize it, too: if every company manipulated every customer this way, trust in online agreements would collapse, just as promising collapses in Kant's example.

But the comparison has limits. Real consent forms are often long, unread and legalistic; “informed consent” can become a box-ticking ritual that protects institutions more than it respects persons. Kant's ideal of fully rational, autonomous agents fits awkwardly with what psychology tells us about how people actually decide: we are tired, distracted and biased. Some ethicists argue for “nudges” that steer people toward better choices, which a strict Kantian might see as disrespect. Where to draw the line between helping and manipulating is a live debate that Kant gives us the language for, but does not settle.

vocabulary.definition: For Kant, the commitment to do what is right because it is right; the only thing good without qualification.
vocabulary.example: Even if her rescue attempt failed, her good will still had full moral worth in Kant's eyes.

vocabulary.definition: The necessity of acting out of respect for the moral law; actions have moral worth for Kant when done from duty, not merely in accordance with it.
vocabulary.example: The shopkeeper gave correct change in accordance with duty, but not from duty, since he was only protecting his business.

vocabulary.definition: The personal principle or policy on which someone acts.
vocabulary.example: “Whenever a test is hard, I'll copy from my neighbor” is a maxim that fails Kant's universalizability test.

vocabulary.definition: A command that applies only if you have a certain goal: “If you want X, do Y.”
vocabulary.example: “If you want to run a marathon, train every week” is a hypothetical imperative.

vocabulary.definition: An unconditional moral command that binds every rational being regardless of their desires; Kant's supreme principle of morality.
vocabulary.example: The categorical imperative forbids lying even when a lie would get you exactly what you want.

vocabulary.definition: The test of whether a maxim could consistently be willed as a law for everyone.
vocabulary.example: Cutting the queue fails universalizability: if everyone did it, there would be no queue to cut.

vocabulary.definition: A being with intrinsic worth that must never be treated merely as a tool for someone else's purposes.
vocabulary.example: Treating the customer as an end in herself means giving her the information she needs to decide.

vocabulary.definition: Literally “self-legislation”: the capacity of a rational being to give itself the moral law; for Kant the ground of human dignity.
vocabulary.example: Kant located human dignity in autonomy, not in wealth, strength or social rank.

thinkingExercise.title: Putting Your Maxims on Trial
thinkingExercise.prompt: Choose three small things you did or were tempted to do this week that you were not entirely comfortable with (a white lie, skipping a fare, ignoring a request for help, a bit of flattery). Run them through Kant's tests.
steps: For each action, write down your maxim as precisely as you can, in the form “When [situation], I will [action] in order to [goal].”
Universalize each maxim. Imagine everyone acted on it. Is that world even conceivable, and could you consistently will to live in it?
Apply the Formula of Humanity. Did anyone get used merely as a means — someone who could not have agreed to what you did if they had understood it?
Now consider the case where Kant's verdict feels wrong to you. Is the problem Kant's theory, or the way you described your maxim? Write a short paragraph explaining which.

summary: Kant held that only a good will is good without qualification, and that actions have moral worth when done from duty, not merely in accordance with it.
Hypothetical imperatives depend on our goals; the categorical imperative commands unconditionally and is the supreme principle of morality.
The Formula of Universal Law tests whether a maxim can be willed as a law for everyone; the lying promise fails because it undermines itself.
The Formula of Humanity forbids treating anyone merely as a means and grounds human dignity in rational autonomy.
The murderer at the door, empty formalism, conflicting duties and coldness are major objections, but Kant's ideas of dignity and respect shaped modern human rights.

quiz.question: Why does Kant say the shopkeeper who gives correct change only to protect his business lacks moral worth?
options: Because the result of his action was bad.
Because he acted in accordance with duty but not from duty.
Because selling bread is not a moral activity.
Because he should have given the child the bread for free.
quiz.explanation: The outcome was right, but his motive was self-interest. Moral worth, for Kant, depends on acting from duty.

quiz.question: Which of these is a categorical imperative?
options: If you want to lose weight, eat less sugar.
If you want to be trusted, keep your promises.
If you want to get promoted, work late.
Do not make promises you intend to break.
quiz.explanation: The last command holds regardless of your goals. The others are hypothetical: they bind only if you want the stated outcome.

quiz.question: Kant thought that the moral worth of an action depends mainly on whether it produces good consequences.
quiz.explanation: Kant located moral worth in the principle and motive of the action. Consequences depend on luck; that is the utilitarian view (Day 61).

quiz.question: Why does the maxim “make false promises when I need money” fail the Formula of Universal Law?
options: Universalized, promises would no longer be believed, so the maxim would defeat itself.
It would make the person who breaks the promise unhappy.
It violates the laws of the state.
Most people would disapprove of it.
quiz.explanation: This is a contradiction in conception: false promising works only if most people keep their promises, so it cannot be a universal law.

quiz.question: According to the Formula of Humanity, what is wrong with ordering coffee from a barista?
options: It treats her as a means, which is always wrong.
It is wrong only if you do not tip.
Nothing, as long as you also respect her as an end and do not deceive or coerce her.
It is wrong because it is a market transaction.
quiz.explanation: Kant forbids treating people *merely* as means. Fair exchanges to which both sides consent are fully compatible with respecting persons.

quiz.question: In his 1797 essay replying to Benjamin Constant, Kant argued that it is wrong to lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding.
quiz.explanation: Kant held truthfulness to be an unconditional duty, a conclusion many readers (and some Kantians, such as Korsgaard) reject.

quiz.question: Which modern practice most directly reflects the Formula of Humanity?
options: Cost-benefit analysis of a new highway
Requiring informed consent before medical research
Ranking job candidates by productivity
Maximizing a company's share price
quiz.explanation: Informed consent ensures participants are treated as autonomous agents who agree to how they are used, not as mere tools.

quiz.question: What does Kant mean by “autonomy”?
options: Doing whatever you feel like
Living independently of other people
Obeying the laws of your country
The capacity of a rational being to give itself the moral law
quiz.explanation: Autonomy means self-legislation by reason. It is not mere freedom to follow desires, which Kant would call heteronomy.

quiz.question: Kant held that the Golden Rule (“do as you would be done by”) is an adequate statement of the supreme moral principle.
quiz.explanation: Kant explicitly called the Golden Rule inadequate because it depends on what particular people happen to want, rather than on what reason requires.

quiz.question: Hegel's charge of “empty formalism” against Kant claims that…
options: the universal law test can approve almost any maxim if it is described cleverly enough
Kant's ethics ignores the role of God
Kant's ethics is too focused on consequences
Kant wrote in an overly formal style
quiz.explanation: The objection is that a purely formal test of consistency gives no real content; how you describe a maxim can change the verdict.

goDeeper.body:
Kant's ethics has had a remarkable second life since the 1970s. John Rawls, whom we meet on Day 82, called his own theory of justice “Kantian” and taught a generation of students to read the *Groundwork* sympathetically. Out of his seminars came the leading contemporary Kantians, including Christine Korsgaard, Onora O'Neill, Barbara Herman and Thomas Hill.

One of their central projects was to show that Kant is not the cold rule-worshipper of caricature. Barbara Herman, for example, argued that the motive of duty can work as a background “limiting condition” rather than the conscious thought behind every action: a kind person can help out of love while also being committed to doing only what is permissible. On this view, the grieving philanthropist is a test case that reveals the motive, not a model of how to live.

A second project concerns the different formulations of the categorical imperative. Kant claimed they are equivalent, but few readers find this obvious. Is the Formula of Universal Law (a test of consistency) really the same as the Formula of Humanity (a demand to respect persons)? Korsgaard argues that both flow from the nature of rational agency itself: when I value my own ends, I must value my capacity to set ends, and consistency then requires me to value that capacity in everyone.

Finally, there is the uncomfortable question of Kant's own views. In his anthropology lectures and other writings he made racist claims about non-Europeans and dismissive claims about women. Scholars disagree about how to handle this. Some, like Pauline Kleingeld, argue that Kant revised his views on race in the 1790s; others, like Charles Mills, argue that his moral community was built on exclusion. Either way, his universal principles have become one of the strongest tools for criticizing those prejudices.

readings.title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
readings.author: Immanuel Kant
readings.note: Short but dense; read Section I (the good will and duty) and the first half of Section II (the imperatives).

readings.title: Creating the Kingdom of Ends
readings.author: Christine M. Korsgaard
readings.note: Influential essays; see “The Right to Lie: Kant on Dealing with Evil” for the murderer-at-the-door case.

readings.title: Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do?
readings.author: Michael J. Sandel
readings.note: Chapter 5 gives a lively, accessible introduction to Kant's ethics with modern examples.

questions: Is an action done from love less morally admirable than the same action done from duty? What would Kant say, and what do you think?
Can you construct a maxim that passes the universal law test but seems obviously wrong? What does that show?
If dignity rests on rational agency, how should Kantians think about babies, people with dementia, and animals?
